title: Ones Written Up to N
statement:
Write down every whole number from 0 to n in decimal. Return how many times the digit 1 appears in total.

A number with several ones counts each of them: 11 adds 2, 111 adds 3.

examples.why: 1, 10, 12 and 13 have one each, 11 has two: 1 + 1 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 6. Counting numbers that contain a 1 would give 5.
Each of the three positions shows a 1 exactly 12 times: ones place in 1, 11, …, 111; tens place in 10–19 and 110–111; hundreds place in 100–111.

hints: Looping over every number up to a billion is too slow. Instead of going number by number, go position by position: how often is the tens digit a 1?

Split n around one position into high (digits to the left), cur (the digit itself) and low (digits to the right). As the numbers count up, the high part cycles, and each full cycle shows that position as 1 exactly 10^k times.
For position 10^k: the count is high · 10^k, plus 10^k more if cur > 1, or low + 1 more if cur = 1, and nothing more if cur = 0.

explain.intuition:
Count by position, not by number. Take the tens place. As you count from 0 upward, the tens digit is 1 for ten numbers (10–19), then not for ninety, then 1 again for 110–119, and so on: a block of ten every hundred. So how many times it shows 1 up to n depends only on how many complete hundreds fit, plus what happens in the last, partial hundred.

For position p = 10^k, split n into high = floor(n / (10p)), cur = floor(n / p) % 10 and low = n % p. The high complete cycles give high · p ones. In the partial cycle: if cur > 1 the whole block of p ones was passed; if cur = 1 you are inside the block and got low + 1 of it; if cur = 0 you have not reached it. Sum this over the at most ten positions.
steps: While p ≤ n: compute high, cur and low for this position.
Add high · p, then add p if cur > 1, or low + 1 if cur = 1.
pitfalls: Counting numbers that contain a 1 instead of counting the digits. 11 must add 2.
Treating cur = 1 like cur > 1. For n = 13 the tens place shows a 1 only in 10–13, which is low + 1 = 4 times, not 10.
In JavaScript, using / without Math.floor. The split only works with integer division.

solutions.title: Recurse on the leading digit
solutions.idea: For n with leading digit d and place value p: the leading position gives p ones (or rest + 1 if d is 1), the d full blocks below give d · f(p − 1), and the remainder gives f(rest).

solutions.title: Count each position directly
solutions.idea: For each place value p, the ones there come from the complete cycles of the digits to the left, plus a partial block decided by the digit at p.

followups: Count how many times any given digit d appears from 0 to n. What changes when d is 0?
Count the ones from a to b instead of from 0 to n.
